decision: Use a shared fsync-backed atomic writer for MissionQueueStore and DurableRequestJournal.
problem: rename-based atomic replacement prevented torn JSON but did not explicitly flush file contents or the containing directory before acknowledging a durable mutation.

reviews.correctness: Preferred write temp -> fsync temp -> rename -> fsync directory so an acknowledged save has stronger crash/power-loss durability semantics.
reviews.robustness_security: Preferred one shared primitive with bounded cleanup over duplicating persistence code; unexpected fsync errors remain fail-closed while known unsupported directory-fsync cases are tolerated after the data file is synced.
reviews.latency_resources_regression: Preferred local fsync over a transactional database or write-ahead service. It adds storage latency only on durable mutations, no network/Qubes dependency, and keeps existing JSON formats and APIs unchanged.

alternatives_rejected: Keep writeFile+rename only: atomic replacement is not the same as explicit durability after acknowledgement.
Move Slice 1 to a transactional database: stronger multi-record semantics but substantially larger operational and regression surface.
Add a separate WAL service: unnecessary process/network lifecycle for the current single-host slice.
qa: Atomic replacement preserves final content and 0600 mode on POSIX.
Temporary state is removed after failed writes.
MissionQueueStore and DurableRequestJournal both use the same primitive.
Existing journal rollback tests continue to prove no phantom in-memory state after persistence failure.
lesson: Atomic rename protects file structure, but durability-sensitive acknowledgements should also define flush semantics explicitly.
